source.title: Do We Always Need the Simplicity Bias? Looking for Optimal Inductive Biases in the Wild
source.authors: Damien Teney; Liang-Ze Jiang; Florin Gogianu; Ehsan Abbasnejad

record.tranche_reason: The study trains models on algorithmic tasks and measures training and test accuracy over optimization, testing grokking with a different training setup and an activation-function intervention.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own grokking experiments in Section 3.5 and Figures 11–13 and 28. Cited results from other work and results on other domains are not included as rows. The plotted training-set-fraction sweep is relevant to V1, but its trend is not described in the text.
record.test_reason: The study trains 1-hidden-layer ReLU MLPs (MSE loss, full-batch GD, no weight decay) on the Power et al. algorithmic tasks and tracks train/test accuracy over steps. The ReLU baseline shows delayed generalization on some tasks. It then shows that learned, task-specific activations essentially remove the delay. This is a different method aimed at whether V1's delay holds.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct: the authors conclude that learned activations eliminate grokking in all their cases. They read this as suggesting the cause is a mismatch between the data and the architecture's inductive biases.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses algorithmic tasks from prior grokking work but trains one-hidden-layer MLPs with width 256, MSE loss, large-batch gradient descent, no weight decay, and random 80/20 splits; it also compares learned activations with ReLUs.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports that outcomes differ between ReLU and learned-activation models; Figure 13 also varies training-data fraction and network width, but the fraction-specific trend is not stated in the text.

fits_no_version.finding: Changing only the activation function (learned sine-like splines) eliminates the grokking delay. The authors attribute grokking to a mismatch between the architecture's inductive bias and the task.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Grokking delay depends on the architecture's inductive bias (activation function); an architecture matched to the task generalizes without delay.

fits_no_version.finding: Some learned-activation models later overfit, with test accuracy decreasing under prolonged training. ReLU models that grok keep high accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: After fast generalization, prolonged training can degrade test accuracy in non-ReLU architectures.

record.problems: For the grokking results, the text gives few numerical outcomes beyond the ∼10× convergence comparison. Several training curves and sweeps are presented only in figures, and the supplied figure extraction does not support recovering their detailed values. The grokking section does not state uncertainty estimates or seed counts.
record.rows_left_out: No additional grokking outcomes were extractable as distinct rows beyond the aggregate results and the Figure 13 sweeps. Figure 28 reports curves for individual algorithmic tasks, but the supplied extraction does not preserve task-to-curve assignments or readable values.

untested.parts: Whether the delay grows as the training set shrinks. Figure 13 plots it, but the text states no trend.
Not tested: no circuit or progress-measure analysis.
Not tested: no non-algorithmic grokking and no init-scale or weight-norm manipulation. An activation-function lever is recorded under fits_no_version.
Not tested. ReLU grokking occurs with no weight decay (MSE loss), but the study does not examine norm, critical dataset size or ungrokking.
Not tested. Training uses full-batch GD rather than Adam, but the study does not frame or control this as an artifact test.

missing.what: ReLU baseline on a+b mod 27 showing delayed test-accuracy rise (the specific grokking instance, ~10× slower than learned activation)

Transfer results: per-column mean accuracy across 22 tasks is 19.9% for ReLU, 61.5% for an activation learned on all tasks, and 54.0% for task-specific activations. This bears on how many tasks ReLU fails within budget.

record.verdict_notes: This is a short section in a broad paper on simplicity bias. Grokking results are mostly figure-only, with no seed counts. Training uses MSE, full-batch GD at lr 1.0, no weight decay and SWA over the last 50 steps. Hyperparameters were tuned for ReLU and reused. Mention of early stopping in E.1 may conflict with tracking curves to 6e4 steps. R5/R6 relinked to none.

versions.untested_parts: The text does not state whether shrinking the training set increases the optimization delay. Figure 13 plots training-set fraction against steps to reach ≥95% test accuracy, but the trend cannot be determined from the supplied figure extraction.
The study does not measure circuit formation, memorizing-component removal, or continuous mechanism-level progress measures.
The grokking experiments are algorithmic tasks; the study does not test grokking on non-algorithmic data or vary initialization scale or weight norm to switch it on or off.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data is studied.
The study does not test a low-norm efficiency account, critical dataset size, or ungrokking. The algorithmic-task setup states that it uses no weight decay.
The study does not compare whether runs converge to the same identifiable algorithm.
The study does not test adaptive-optimizer instability or floating-point/softmax artifacts as explanations of grokking.

rows.note: This is the authors' aggregate description of ReLU outcomes across the tested algorithmic tasks; it reports both non-generalizing and grokking cases.
rows.check: Aggregate over 22 tasks. ReLU nets 'either never generalize (test accuracy ∼0) or grok'. Grokking is observed on a subset of tasks; the rest never generalize within 6e4 steps. No per-task counts are given in the text.

rows.measure: Training and test accuracy over optimization; delayed convergence
rows.baseline: ReLU networks on the same tasks
rows.value: The learned-activation models converge faster and/or reach higher test accuracy; the authors say they eliminate grokking in all their tested cases. On modular addition mod 27, convergence is ∼10× faster than with ReLUs.
rows.note: This is a changed-activation condition, not evidence that the usual ReLU setup lacks grokking.
rows.check: Correct as a changed-activation condition. The authors say learned activations 'essentially eliminate grokking', with ∼10× faster convergence on a+b mod 27. The learned activation is the study's own method, but here it serves as an intervention on whether the delay occurs. Baseline hyperparameters were tuned on ReLU and reused unchanged.
